short_answer: Yes, especially from Second Temple literature; in his view, the idea is much later than the Bronze Age or early Iron Age.
expanded_answer: Heiser drew especially from Second Temple literature and related later Jewish traditions, and he treats that as Heiser's real area of expertise. In his argument, the divine-council framework does not belong to the Bronze Age or early Iron Age, and Heiser's Exodus material shows serious Egyptological errors.

question: Did Michael Heiser know how to read Egyptian hieroglyphs?
short_answer: No.
expanded_answer: He did not know how to read Egyptian hieroglyphs. Someone who could read Egyptian should have recognized that Beni Hassan is an Arabic place-name rather than an Egyptian personal name, and the mistaken identification reinforced that conclusion.

question: Is there anything right in Heiser's divine-council view?
short_answer: Heiser is partly right about Second Temple Jewish belief, but wrong to project that theology back across all biblical history.
expanded_answer: Heiser is right that many Second Temple Jews believed in a council of gods, but wrong to treat that as universal across all biblical history. He regards that move as anachronistic extrapolation and says some of the proof texts, such as the judgment on Egypt in Exodus 12, are badly misread.

question: What is your opinion of the prosperity gospel circling around the world?
short_answer: It is carnal, works-based, manipulative theology that turns faith into a way to force God and then blames sufferers.
expanded_answer: Prosperity teaching is denounced as a carnal, works-based distortion of the gospel that turns faith into a mechanism for acquiring health, wealth, and status. It makes God subservient to faith, manipulates God, violates the second commandment, and blames suffering people for not having enough faith.

question: Did the temple of Thoth at Tuna el-Gebel contain thousands of mummified ibises and baboons as offerings?
short_answer: Yes, though the temple is late and less interesting to him.
expanded_answer: The Thoth temple contained many mummified animals, including ibises and baboons, with some other animals as well. It is described as a very late, Ptolemaic-period temple and therefore less central to his own interests.

question: Would Yahweh's lack of a theogony be unique among gods of Egypt or the broader ancient Near East?
short_answer: Individual gods may lack origin stories, but an entire Yahweh religious system without a theogony is distinctive.
expanded_answer: A theogony is an origin or birth account for a god, and not every Egyptian deity has one. The distinctiveness, in his view, is not that one specific god lacks an origin story, but that Yahweh worship as a whole lacks a theogony in a wider ancient Near Eastern setting where such stories are the norm.

question: How do I contact you to set up an appearance?
short_answer: Facebook is best, with Discord also possible, and short messages work better than long life-story emails.
expanded_answer: Facebook is the best route because that is where he handles most appearance and chat arrangements, while Discord can also work. He avoids email for this because people often send very long life stories before a short question, and he prefers brief, direct messages.

question: How do I make a collab video?
short_answer: Something like Zoom, Google Meet, or StreamYard can work, and he uses OBS Studio with StreamYard.
expanded_answer: A caller can use a video meeting or streaming platform such as Zoom, Meet, or StreamYard. For his own setup, he usually uses StreamYard for collaborations and OBS Studio for video work because the two work well together.

question: Are you a ham radio operator?
short_answer: Yes. His certificates had just arrived, and he gave his call sign.
expanded_answer: The ham radio certificates had arrived that same week, and he identified his call sign as Victor Alpha 7 Zulu Delta Fox Trot. He also expected an advanced certificate soon.

question: Would you be willing to take young seminary students under your wing?
short_answer: Yes in principle, but it would be consulting work with a fee, and he is not willing to go through a full seminary employment process.
expanded_answer: He is willing in principle, but mentoring seminary students would become paid consulting work. He is not interested in going through a seminary's full employment or credentialing process for a small adjunct-like role, especially when institutions demand extensive interviews, references, and sealed transcripts.

question: Where do scholars get the idea that El distributed lands to other gods?
short_answer: Deuteronomy 32:8 is the main text, but he considered the "sons of Elohim" versus "sons of Israel" reading unresolved.
expanded_answer: Deuteronomy 32:8 is the main source, and the debate depends on whether the text reads "sons of Israel" or "sons of Elohim." The Septuagint and one Dead Sea Scroll support the divine-sons reading, while the Masoretic and Samaritan traditions support Israel. He saw support for both readings and explicitly declined to choose between them.

question: With AI, quantum computing, and new subsurface scanning, how optimistic are you about another archaeological boom?
short_answer: He is cautious: AI and quantum computing are not naturally paired, and archaeology already has more identified sites than resources to dig them.
expanded_answer: AI and quantum computing are very different technologies, with AI using feedback loops and quantum computing testing multiple states, so he is skeptical that pairing them will transform archaeology. He is also wary of AI hallucinations and thinks archaeology already has a larger problem of limited resources than of insufficient site identification.

question: Could subsurface analysis technology make huge inroads in seeing what is hidden under dirt?
short_answer: Scanning technologies have promise, but the main bottleneck is still money, preservation, staff, guards, storage, and academic infrastructure.
expanded_answer: He sees more promise in scanning technology than in the computational backend, but says technology is not the main constraint. Satellite archaeology has already identified far more Egyptian sites than can be excavated, and digging them responsibly requires funding, guards, storage, preservation plans, academic departments, and people to process the data.

question: How is Itjtawy spelled?
short_answer: An approximate spelling was shown on screen, but the TXT transcript does not preserve it reliably.
expanded_answer: The name had just been used for the Middle Kingdom capital. He apparently typed an approximate spelling on screen, but the text captions preserve only the automatic-transcript form "Ichitawi," so the displayed spelling cannot be verified from the TXT source.

question: Are there any books on the ancient-world culture of the Old Testament patriarchs?
short_answer: Richard Hess's *Israelite Religions* is the recommended primer.
expanded_answer: Richard Hess's *Israelite Religions* is the concise recommendation. It is described as the best book and a good primer for the cultural world of the Old Testament patriarchs.

question: Was Arius a Trinitarian?
short_answer: No. Arius was non-Trinitarian and specifically Arian in theology.
expanded_answer: Arius was not Trinitarian because Arius held that there is one God, the Father, and that Jesus Christ was the first creation of God. In that view, Jesus then makes the world, but he is not God in the Trinitarian sense.

question: Did Arius think Jesus was divine and the Son of God?
short_answer: Arius treated Jesus as the first and highest created being, with `Son of God` understood biologically rather than as a divine title.
expanded_answer: Arius understood "Son of God" biologically, meaning Jesus was generated or created by God rather than eternally divine. Thus Jesus could be the highest created being, but still as created as the earth or humanity and therefore not Trinitarian.

question: What is your scholarly opinion of MythVision and Derek Lambert's claims about the origins of religion?
short_answer: The argument is parallelomania and a genetic fallacy: finding parallels does not prove one religion caused another.
expanded_answer: The argument finds parallels between religions and then treats those parallels as proof of origin, which he calls parallelomania. He frames it as a genetic or association fallacy, emphasizing that correlation or prior similarity does not establish causation.

question: What is your opinion of IP on an intellectual level?
short_answer: IP is one of the better apologists, reads a lot, asks subject-matter experts, and is intellectually honest, though sometimes overly generous to opponents.
expanded_answer: The assessment is positive personally and intellectually: IP is treated as one of the better apologists, with philosophy training, broad reading, and a willingness to consult subject-matter experts. IP listened after criticism and improved, though his intellectual honesty can make him more generous to opponents than Dr. Falk would be.

question: What do you think of the Gosford glyphs?
short_answer: They are badly done forgeries that real Egyptologists have already analyzed.
expanded_answer: The Gosford glyphs are forgeries, and not subtle ones. Real Egyptologists and field experts have analyzed them, leaving no real question in his mind that they are fabricated.

question: Do we know why God caused 70,000 people to die because David took a census?
short_answer: The response did not address why; it only suggested a plague or outbreak as the physical mechanism.
expanded_answer: The theological reason for the judgment is not explained in the response. Instead, a plague or similar outbreak is proposed as the likely physical mechanism, with cholera and pneumonic plague given as examples of diseases that can kill very large numbers quickly.

question: Is CB radio still a thing?
short_answer: Yes, people still use it, but licenses and restrictions apply depending on band and country.
expanded_answer: CB radio still exists and people still use it, but licensing and restrictions depend on the country and radio band. He distinguishes CB, GMRS, and amateur bands, noting that he can listen to CB with ham equipment but cannot broadcast there under amateur privileges.

question: What are the primary sources for the Council of Nicaea?
short_answer: The council proceedings and resolutions are the closest primary sources, though they are not a full blow-by-blow transcript.
expanded_answer: Nicaea is one of the councils for which proceedings or resolutions were written and copied, unlike some other councils. They are contemporary and therefore the closest available primary sources, but they preserve resolutions rather than a complete transcript of every exchange.

question: Are there commentaries or study Bibles that take a late date for the Exodus?
short_answer: Some do. A few commentaries and study Bibles present late-date options, though most still favor the early date.
expanded_answer: Some commentators and study Bibles do include late-date options, although most still prefer the early date partly because of publisher pressure. Examples include study Bibles that present both early and late timelines, along with an anecdote about Kenneth Kitchen sharply criticizing an early-date chart sent to him for review.

question: Can you assess the ESV Archaeology Study Bible for a young person interested in archaeology?
short_answer: He could not assess it because he did not own that edition.
expanded_answer: He initially thought he had the ESV Archaeology Study Bible, but returned with a CSB study Bible instead and therefore declined to evaluate the ESV volume. He only noted that the CSB edition is generally attractive, has good pictures, and uses an early Exodus date.

question: Can you explain how the pyramids were built?
short_answer: The basic answer is boats, sledges, ropes, and pulley or lever systems rather than a lost mystery.
expanded_answer: The stones were transported by boat using displacement, brought close to the pyramid by Nile channels and ports, then moved on land by sledges, ropes, and pulley or lever systems. Lost-technology explanations are rejected, and experimental archaeology is used to show how Bronze Age tools could move, carve, drill, and place the stones.

question: What are your thoughts on `Heliopolis of the South`, `Iunu Shema`, and Thebes?
short_answer: The title is `Heka Iunu Shema`, ruler of Heliopolis of the South, and it is treated as a religious title.
expanded_answer: The expression parses as `Heka Iunu Shema`, meaning ruler of Heliopolis of the South. It is part of a name or title connected with Thebes and religious geography rather than a major separate problem.

question: Are you a Freemason?
short_answer: No.
expanded_answer: The answer is limited to a direct denial: he is not a Freemason. No additional explanation or related argument is given before the stream moves to the next question.

question: Is there a good book comparing old-earth creationism, theistic evolution, and young-earth creationism?
short_answer: Start with Scripture itself rather than jumping first into systems defending any one camp.
expanded_answer: Beginning with old-earth, young-earth, or theistic-evolution systems is unhelpful because they are concordist attempts to harmonize science and biblical origins. Genesis 1-11 is better approached on its own terms as religious prolegomena and mytho-history, and some of John Walton's earlier Genesis work is useful for that framing.

question: Have you tried cold-brew coffee?
short_answer: Yes, but if he wants twice the caffeine he prefers an Italiano coffee maker.
expanded_answer: He has tried cold brew and does not have much stomach-acid trouble from coffee. If he wants a strong caffeine hit, he prefers an Italiano coffee maker, joking that two pots left him wired for about 36 hours.

question: Did Kenneth Kitchen ever see *Patterns of Evidence*?
short_answer: No, but Kitchen knew David Rohl's work and had a very low opinion of both Rohl and his ideas.
expanded_answer: Kitchen never watched *Patterns of Evidence*, but he already knew David Rohl's work and strongly rejected it. He recalls Kitchen calling Rohl a time waster and dilettante, and says Kitchen had contempt for both Rohl and the ideas associated with him.

question: What do evangelicals get wrong about the Catholic-versus-Protestant Reformation issue?
short_answer: They often focus on symptoms such as the pope or indulgences, while the deeper issue was the storehouse of good works and related soteriology.
expanded_answer: People should read the Luther and Erasmus debates rather than rely only on summaries. The Reformation dispute was not fundamentally about the pope, Marian dogmas, or indulgences as isolated issues, but about the `thesaurus ecclesiae`, supererogatory works, and whether righteousness comes from God alone.

question: Does reading R. C. Sproul count as reading Calvin?
short_answer: No; Sproul condenses Calvin for lay readers and loses much of Calvin's nuance.
expanded_answer: Sproul was a Calvinist, but his explanations simplify Calvin for lay readers. That compression loses qualifications, tensions, and nuance found in the six-volume *Institutes*, so people who call themselves Calvinists or criticize Calvin should read Calvin directly.

question: What is a Christian nationalist, and are you one?
short_answer: No; Christian nationalism uses law to impose Old Testament legalism, racism, and cultural control.
expanded_answer: Christian nationalism is rejected and defined as applying Old Testament law through government, with racism, legalism, and enforced monoculture added in practice. Examples included banning mixed marriages, regulating worship times, suppressing modern culture, and using law to force behavior beyond what Scripture requires. Asked whether that program would outlaw public teaching of evolution, he could only say that it possibly or probably would.

question: Could the original Eden have been in the Persian Gulf coast near Iraq and then flooded?
short_answer: Probably; the original Eden was likely in what archaeologists call Sealand, much of which has been reclaimed by the Persian Gulf.
expanded_answer: The original Eden was likely in the region archaeologists call Sealand. Much of that area has been reclaimed by the Persian Gulf as Mesopotamian coastline shifted and low-lying land was subsumed.

question: What do you say about the Israelites passing through the Red Sea?
short_answer: It was historical but happened at the Sea of Reeds in the northwest Sinai, not at the modern Red Sea or Gulf of Aqaba.
expanded_answer: The crossing was historical but at `Yam Suph`, the Sea of Reeds, in the northwest Sinai near the Pelusiac estuary, not the Gulf of Aqaba. He links this to Egyptian geographic texts placing it between Pi-Ramesses and Tjaru, and discusses nearby lakes, wind setdown, Pi-hahiroth, Baal-zephon, and the Road of Horus fortresses.

question: Did Egypt have an Iron Age?
short_answer: Yes, but the chronological Iron Age label differs from Egypt's later technological adoption of iron tools in the Third Intermediate Period.
expanded_answer: Egypt can be placed in the Iron Age chronologically around the end of Dynasty 20 or about 1000 BC for comparison with neighboring cultures, but technologically it remained heavily bronze-using for longer. Egypt's proper technological Iron Age begins later in the Third Intermediate Period when iron tools become common.

episode_title: I Can't Believe We've Been Doing This For 6 Months
question: When is he going to write a lay-level book on the evidence for the Exodus?
short_answer: A lay Exodus book remains desirable, but time, funding, and his non-academic day job make it unrealistic in the near term.
expanded_answer: The obstacle is time: regular manual-labor work, channel videos, and Friday livestreams leave little writing room. A funded sabbatical had been hoped for, especially for a plagues book, but the support was not enough to make that practical, so a lay Exodus-evidence book remains a later hope rather than a near-term project.

episode_title: I Can't Believe We've Been Doing This For 6 Months

question: Had he heard of the Niese of Power scandal, where a delayed baptism was followed by deleted Christian content?
short_answer: No. Without the details, it only suggested that the person may not have been ready for baptism.
expanded_answer: He had not heard of the scandal and avoided judging the details. On the limited description, a delayed baptism followed by deleting Christian content would tend to confirm that the person was not ready for baptism, matching the prior caution against rushing candidates.

question: Do early human diets provide a guide for modern diets?
short_answer: We are still not sure enough about Homo sapiens diet to treat it as a simple guide for what people should eat now.
expanded_answer: Ancient Homo sapiens diet is not known well enough to make it normative for modern eating, and even if it were known, ancient survival food was not necessarily ideal. Modern food can be more nutritious, and some past foods included toxic or starvation-ration items, so ancestral diet is a poor guide by itself.

question: What fish are in the aquarium?
short_answer: There are no fish: the aquarium has mostly cherry shrimp, plus a couple of nerite snails and plants.
expanded_answer: The aquarium contains no fish. It has mostly cherry shrimp, specifically Neocaridina, along with a couple of nerite snails and many plants, with about ten shrimp estimated at the time of the stream.

question: What about Chinese noodles?
short_answer: Chinese noodles are fine, but he does not cook much with them.
expanded_answer: Chinese noodles are fine, and chow mein is an occasional meal. The limit is personal cooking interest: Chinese cuisine is not an area he spends much time cooking or exploring.

question: Does Galatians mean people who want water baptism should not be stopped?
short_answer: Only genuine saved converts should be baptized; people who are not ready or not in the faith should wait.
expanded_answer: That kind of appeal assumes the person is already saved and sincerely seeking baptism. Genuine candidates should not be stopped, but people treating baptism frivolously, collecting baptisms, or not yet being valid converts should wait.

question: How does monarchial Trinitarianism differ from other models of the Trinity?
short_answer: In his description, it is the three coequal, coeternal persons organized as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, contrasted with subordinationist, social, eternal-generation, and qualitative models.
expanded_answer: Monarchial Trinitarianism is defined here as the three coequal, coeternal persons of one essence organizing themselves as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It is contrasted with subordinationist models, social Trinitarianism, eternal generation, and qualitative approaches that explain the persons or divine essence differently.

question: Will Christians learn about the Trinity in heaven?
short_answer: Yes. Believers will continue exploring that mystery eternally, even without exhausting it.
expanded_answer: Christians will be able to explore the deep mysteries of the Trinity for all eternity. Even in heaven they will remain limited human beings, so they will not exhaust the subject, but they will have eternity to keep learning.

question: When will his article on the genealogies of Genesis be published?
short_answer: It will eventually be published when he has time to finish it, but he has many writing commitments.
expanded_answer: The article will be published eventually, but only when he has time to finish it amid other obligations. Peer-reviewed articles take far more precision, citation work, and effort than books, and he has several long-running writing commitments competing for time.

question: What is the Berlin pedestal theory?
short_answer: It is a disputed claim that a Berlin Museum pedestal contains the word Israel and supports an early Exodus date.
expanded_answer: The theory concerns a column-base pedestal in the Berlin Museum, associated with an alleged reading of "Israel." The reading is criticized as strained, and early-Exodus advocates are said to treat it as evidence while resisting criticism.

question: Does he intend to publish the Berlin pedestal paper in another journal?
short_answer: Yes. He intends to publish it eventually and has already dusted it off for another look.
expanded_answer: He does intend to publish the Berlin pedestal paper eventually and has already taken another look at it. The first six months of the year had been crowded with other writing commitments, so publication was not imminent.

question: Is it a problem to keep research up to date because publication takes so long?
short_answer: It can be a problem for time-sensitive work, but most of his work is not time-sensitive, and peer reviewers often point out new research to add.
expanded_answer: Delayed publication can matter for time-sensitive research, but most of what he publishes is not that time-sensitive. If something cutting-edge is missed, peer reviewers often point it out and the author adds it, which is one reason the review process itself can take a long time.

question: What should someone do with a gap year between undergraduate and graduate study?
short_answer: Keep studying and use the time intentionally, especially by strengthening English grammar.
expanded_answer: The advice is to continue studying, especially by strengthening English grammar before graduate work. Graduate school involves far more writing than exams, so mastering basics such as commas, semicolons, and clear academic prose will prevent writing from dragging down assignments.

question: Do Christians and Jews have a divine right to the land of Israel?
short_answer: Christians do not have such a claim; the biblical land promise is tied specifically to the descendants of Jacob.
expanded_answer: Christians do not have a claim because the land promise was made to the sons of Jacob, not to Christians as such. Modern Jews, as descendants of Jacob, are said to have a claim and many never fully left the land, though that is distinguished from the separate question of whether to call it a divine right.

question: How are demons and aliens different from each other?
short_answer: In his framework, demons are a known spiritual category, whereas alien life remains unproven and speculative.
expanded_answer: Demons are spirits and, in this framework, known to exist, while alien life may or may not exist and would probably not be spiritual if it did. Some alleged alien encounters could be demonic deception, but that would require an actual deceptive message, not merely an unexplained light or sighting.

question: Could some unknown aerial sightings also be angels?
short_answer: Yes, it is possible, but an unexplained sighting by itself does not prove whether it is angelic, demonic, alien, or something else.
expanded_answer: Angelic sightings are possible, but unexplained aerial phenomena do not identify themselves. A bright light or fast-moving object could confuse or frighten someone without proving it is an angel, demon, alien, or something else, so the evidence must not be overread.

question: How do UFOs seem to break the laws of physics?
short_answer: We do not really know that they do break physics; the reports are difficult to explain with current assumptions.
expanded_answer: We do not know whether UFOs actually break physics; they may only appear to do so because of unknown materials or technology. Hard turns and sonic booms are examples where better design or energy redirection could change expectations, while angels or demons in extra dimensions are treated as a separate question with its own rules.

question: If intelligent alien life were detected, why would that worry some Christians?
short_answer: The worry is not clear to him, but theologians are discussing the issue more because of organic compounds and possible life signs, not just UFO reports.
expanded_answer: Alien life would not necessarily affect faith, and the current theological discussion is driven more by scientific findings than by UFO stories. Mars and exoplanet observations of organic compounds or possible biological precursors make people wonder whether life might exist elsewhere, which has prompted more open discussion.

question: What is the relationship between the physical world and the spiritual world, and do they influence each other?
short_answer: The interaction is unclear, though they do interact, and even the physical world is hard to define at a fundamental level.
expanded_answer: How the physical and spiritual worlds interact is unclear, though interaction is affirmed. Even the physical world is hard to define at its deepest levels, with mass, atoms, electron shells, quarks, and gluons used as examples of how strange the physical world already is.

question: What is dark matter, and is it the power of Jesus or connected to spirits?
short_answer: Dark matter is a hypothesis for gravity effects, not something he identifies with Jesus' power or with spirits.
expanded_answer: Dark matter is posited because galaxies move in ways that seem to require extra gravitational effects. It may be undetectable matter or perhaps not matter at all; the math suggests something reacts to gravity, but too little is known to identify it with spirits, and spirits are not treated as made of dark matter.

question: Did Egyptians, Romans, and other ancient nations have UFO sightings or something similar?
short_answer: Ancient people did see unexplained phenomena, but they interpreted them through categories such as omens rather than modern UFO language.
expanded_answer: Seeing unexplained phenomena is not new, and ancient Egyptians, Romans, and others did have interpretive categories for such things. Rather than calling them UFOs, they tended to read them as omens or other meaningful signs and draw inferences from them.

question: Why does Exodus prescribe stoning the ox instead of cutting its throat, and how does one stone an ox?
short_answer: Stoning prevents anyone from profiting from the meat of a dangerous animal that killed someone; the method is essentially throwing large sharp stones.
expanded_answer: The dangerous-ox law is read as part of lex talionis, with the point that a killer animal should not become profitable meat. Cutting the throat would preserve usable meat, while stoning leaves the blood in the flesh and makes the carcass practically inedible; the method is essentially using large sharp stones, as in human stoning.

question: What does "our body is a temple" have to do with rituals, laws, and sacrifice?
short_answer: The comparison is a category error: the body as temple concerns living unto Christ with the Spirit in us, while ritual law and sacrifice were fulfilled in Christ.
expanded_answer: The body-as-temple language is about the Spirit dwelling in believers and about living unto Christ, not about reinstating temple ritual, law, or sacrifice. Attempts to map the phrase onto ritual obligations are treated as a category error because Christ has already fulfilled the sacrificial system.

question: Should Christians still think in terms of clean and unclean ritual categories?
short_answer: Ritual-law categories generally do not apply after Christ, but some ritual laws overlap with moral law and still need discernment.
expanded_answer: Clean and unclean are treated as part of the ritual law, which served as a schoolteacher until righteousness was achieved through Christ. The caveat is that some ritual-law items also venture into moral law, so categories marked as abominations should be examined carefully rather than dismissed automatically.

question: Is it sinful to smoke?
short_answer: Smoking itself is not usually sinful, but it is foolish and can become sinful when it harms others or misuses money needed by the family.
expanded_answer: Smoking is not inherently sinful, giving historical examples of Christians who smoked, but it is foolish because the health risks are now known. It becomes sinful when it harms others through second-hand smoke, affects pregnancy, or diverts needed family money into a damaging personal habit.

question: Who is the person devoted to herem in Leviticus 27, and is Leviticus 27:29 proof that Israelites practiced human sacrifice?
short_answer: Leviticus 27 is about difficult vows and devoted-to-destruction law, not proof that approved Israelite human sacrifice was intended.
expanded_answer: Leviticus 27 is read in the context of difficult vows and valuations, with the chapter providing a way to pay instead of carrying out a destructive vow involving a person. The herem language is treated as devoted-to-destruction law, not as proof that Israelite human sacrifice was approved, and Jephthah is used as the kind of situation where a way out existed.

question: Were the slaves in the biography of Ahmose Israelites?
short_answer: Yes, many likely were Israelites because Avaris was in Goshen, though other people lived there too.
expanded_answer: The text is identified as the biography of Ahmose son of Abana, which describes the siege of Avaris and the taking of slaves. Many of those slaves were likely Israelites because Avaris was the principal city of Goshen, but other people lived there too, so the group would not have been exclusively Israelite.

question: Why do ancient Jewish and early Christian interpretations either deny Jephthah sacrificed his daughter or criticize the sacrifice as immoral?
short_answer: The sacrifice was immoral, and the text is about not making rash vows; Jephthah had ways out but did not take them.
expanded_answer: The sacrifice was immoral, and that is treated as the point of the text: Jephthah made a rash vow he did not need to make. God would have given victory anyway, grace and lawful escape were available, and Jephthah's pride and ego kept him from taking those ways out.

question: Why had Angel Studios' Mormon ownership received so little attention from Christians?
short_answer: Christian media projects may share distribution relationships with Angel Studios, giving them little incentive to emphasize the ownership issue.
expanded_answer: The answer points to Christian media projects sharing distribution channels with Angel Studios. Gesher Media's Ark of the Covenant film is given as an example of a Christian project being distributed through Angel Studios, helping explain why people in the same media network might not emphasize the company's ownership.

question: Did the same people who promoted *Samson* buy the rights to distribute *Animal Farm*?
short_answer: Yes.
expanded_answer: Yes. Angel Studios did not create *Animal Farm*; it bought the film's distribution rights.

question: What is the best movie portrayal of Jesus?
short_answer: His favorite is *The Gospel of John* because it is very true to the Gospel it portrays.
expanded_answer: *The Gospel of John* is chosen because it is long, almost like a miniseries, and the truest to the Gospel it portrays. Its focus on one Gospel rather than a four-Gospel harmonization is treated as a strength, and it is judged far better than *The Passion of the Christ* despite earning far less.

question: Why did Jesus call the Canaanite woman a dog, or have we misconstrued the meaning of his response?
short_answer: Jesus was using the disciples' own pejorative language to teach them that salvation is for Gentiles as well as Jews.
expanded_answer: The key question is who Jesus was addressing indirectly: the disciples, who as first-century Jews would know "dogs" as a common pejorative for Gentiles. In this reading, Jesus uses their own language to overturn their us-versus-them mentality and show that salvation is for Gentiles as well as Jews.

question: What Old Testament movies does he recommend besides *The Ten Commandments*?
short_answer: No alternative is recommended; *The Ten Commandments* remains his preferred Exodus film.
expanded_answer: No other Old Testament movie is named. He instead says *The Ten Commandments* is by far the best Exodus film, while noting that its long love story could have been cut and its Red Sea scene was historically inaccurate; he nevertheless praises how much Egyptian material it got right.

question: To refute the pyramids-Orion conspiracy, can they dig where Sirius is supposed to be?
short_answer: No. The Orion theory is rejected as recent and unsupported, and the proposed alignment is impractical with no ancient evidence behind it.
expanded_answer: The Orion alignment theory is described as a recent idea from the 1980s, not an ancient one. It is rejected because the claimed alignment depends on standing far away with difficult parallax and visibility conditions, and because there is no ancient evidence that the pyramids were built for that purpose.

question: Would an ancient Egyptian man have been allowed to make offerings for a father who was a condemned traitor or serious criminal?
short_answer: Yes. Execution was the punishment in this life, but proper burial, mummification, and funerary offerings could still follow.
expanded_answer: Execution was the earthly penalty, not a reason to deny private funerary rights. Burial, mummification, and offerings were privately paid, and Pentawer, involved in the assassination of Ramesses III, was cited as an example of a serious traitor who could still receive proper burial.

question: Was any crime considered serious enough in Egypt to bring afterlife punishment?
short_answer: Explicit afterlife punishment appears late, especially in the Third Intermediate Period, and earlier problems were often treated as ritually mitigable.
expanded_answer: Most dangers could be mitigated by magic spells, and afterlife punishment does not really appear in Egyptian religion until the Third Intermediate Period. That development was connected indirectly to Atenist influence, where divine punishment was imagined as taking place in this life.

question: Can God rewrite the past so that a real event never happened, or vice versa?
short_answer: God could do so in principle, but there is no apparent need because providence already governs history without that step.
expanded_answer: God has the power in principle, but such a power would have no necessity because God already orders the present and knows every possible future. Since God is outside time and can arrange history as he wills from the start, there is no reason that rewriting the past would ever need to be exercised.

question: What is inside the large void in the Great Pyramid?
short_answer: Probably loose or low-density fill, not a hidden chamber, passage, or sensational discovery.
expanded_answer: No one knows for certain, but the safest guess offered was loose stone, low-density stone, or gravel fill rather than a lost chamber or passageway. The void looks amorphous rather than architectural, which fits comparison to known gravel fill in some pyramids.

question: On the Karnak relief map of the Way of Horus, was Gardiner's inscription C a separate fortress name?
short_answer: Probably not; Gardiner likely mistook parts of Tjaru for two fortresses and treated gouging as an inscription.
expanded_answer: Tjaru was one composite border fortress divided by a river or canal, not two separately named forts. Because Gardiner worked before later excavation clarified that point, he likely assumed a missing name where there was no separate inscription; the apparent gouging could also reflect erosion on reconstructed blocks rather than deliberate erasure.

question: Which Christian emperor, king, or queen was closest to being the ideal Christian ruler?
short_answer: It is almost impossible to answer because even good rulers have serious stains; bad rulers are easier to identify.
expanded_answer: The only easy ideal answer would be Jesus, but that does not really answer the secular-ruler question. For earthly rulers, even good Christian rulers have public or private sins and historical stains, so identifying the best one is far harder than identifying obviously bad rulers.

question: How many semesters of biblical Hebrew and Koine Greek are needed to be ready for a PhD in Old Testament or New Testament?
short_answer: Old Testament usually requires two years of Hebrew, New Testament three years of Greek, and some programs require both.
expanded_answer: The requirement was framed by field: Old Testament doctoral work generally requires two years of Hebrew, while New Testament doctoral work generally requires three years of Greek. Depending on the school, a student may need both languages, so the practical answer can be two years of Hebrew plus three years of Greek.

question: Are online MA programs in theology or philosophy advisable when someone cannot attend full-time in person?
short_answer: Online graduate programs are less than ideal because graduate education is professional development, not just information transfer.
expanded_answer: Master's and doctoral programs are meant to build scholarly relationships, habits, recommendations, and professional interaction. Online programs can transfer information, but they usually do not let professors know a student well enough or provide the face-to-face formation that graduate education is supposed to give.

question: What motivates or inspires David to write?
short_answer: After the joke answer of insomnia, the deeper drive is characters and how they react inside a created world.
expanded_answer: Insomnia often gives him writing time, but the deeper motivation is entering the minds of characters. He likes setting up a theme, a problem, and a world, then seeing how the characters behave within those constraints.

question: How did Pharaoh govern Egypt while traveling to perform religious duties?
short_answer: Pharaoh delegated to viziers and a large bureaucracy; the vizier could manage state affairs while Pharaoh performed rituals.
expanded_answer: Egypt had a massive bureaucracy that could keep the state running while Pharaoh was absent. The vizier, or sometimes two viziers, could act with delegated authority, use the seal ring, enact laws at Pharaoh's discretion, and manage affairs while Pharaoh traveled temple to temple for rituals.

question: Was there anything only Pharaoh could do?
short_answer: Yes. Only Pharaoh could serve as high priest of every cult and appoint the crown prince.
expanded_answer: Pharaoh alone could act as high priest of every Egyptian cult, a role the vizier was not permitted to fill. Succession was also a royal-only act: a vizier could not designate the heir or appoint the crown prince.

question: Were viziers allowed to start wars with other nations?
short_answer: No. Viziers could mount a civil defense, but they could not start wars or military campaigns.
expanded_answer: The vizier was not in command of the military in a way that allowed him to launch foreign wars. A vizier could organize civil defense during an invasion and handle ordinary court business, law, and taxation disputes, but could not start campaigns on his own.

question: Is division among Christians due to powers and principalities?
short_answer: No. Division is because of sin; not everything is demons or forces of darkness.
expanded_answer: Demons or dark powers were rejected as the explanation for every division. Much Christian division comes from human sin: people doing evil, disregarding others, and behaving badly toward one another without needing a demonic cause.

question: Could a vizier judge criminals?
short_answer: It depended on the case. Viziers could judge lesser civil or financial matters, but capital cases belonged to the king.
expanded_answer: Lesser cases were distinguished from life-and-death cases. A vizier could adjudicate civil matters, financial disputes, and petty matters, but capital offenses were reserved for the king because cases involving death belonged to royal judgment.

question: Were there two viziers in ancient Egypt?
short_answer: Sometimes. It depends on period, with one vizier in some eras and two in others, including the New Kingdom.
expanded_answer: The number depends on the period: earlier periods such as the Middle Kingdom had one vizier, while the New Kingdom had two. The change was explained as an administrative response to growth, especially as the Delta became more heavily occupied and Egypt needed more regional administration.

question: What is the Faulk writing unit?
short_answer: It is a 384-word daily count, enough to write 100,000 words in ten months.
expanded_answer: The 384-word unit came from calculating how much daily writing a 100,000-word Liverpool PhD thesis would require to finish in ten months. It functions as a useful pacing tool because it is about a page and a half, easy to accumulate, and scalable for books or theses.

question: Does sin nature cause people to feel pain when standing in God's presence?
short_answer: Yes. Sinful humans can react with fear, anxiety, or pain before holiness, often called the trauma of holiness.
expanded_answer: Theologians call this the trauma of holiness: God's holiness and energies provoke fear and distress in sinful humans, which is why angels often begin by saying not to fear. One theory of hell similarly connects the pain to the interaction between divine holiness and the sinner's own condition.

question: Is repetition an underused or misunderstood writing technique?
short_answer: It can be effective, especially in dialogue or tag phrases, but modern readers have low tolerance for overuse.
expanded_answer: Repetition once had more literary acceptance, but modern readers tolerate very little of it. It can still work when used sparingly, especially in dialogue, alliteration, or recurring verbal markers that identify a character, but constant repetition was discouraged.

question: Is it sinful to attend non-denominational churches?
short_answer: No, as long as they are real Christian churches, though some non-denominational churches have serious problems.
expanded_answer: Attending a non-denominational church is not sinful if it is genuinely part of the universal Christian church. Some such churches have serious problems, just as some denominational churches do, so a person needs to know what they are actually joining.

question: Is it sinful to start your own non-denominational church?
short_answer: It depends on motive: starting one to preach Christ is not wrong, but ego or self-serving motives would change the assessment.
expanded_answer: The motive controls the answer. Starting a church to spread the gospel is not wrong, but starting one to avoid accountability, taxes, discipline, or scrutiny over immoral conduct would be sinful.

question: In Mark 12:28-34, how high a compliment was Jesus giving the scribe?
short_answer: It was more recognition than compliment: Jesus recognized that the scribe understood Torah and was on the right path.
expanded_answer: The passage was read as Jesus acknowledging that the scribe understood the intent of Torah, not merely the letter of the law. The phrase "not far from the kingdom of God" shows the scribe was close because he understood living Torah, but it was not simply flattery.

question: Could Merneptah's reference to Israel being laid waste refer to the plague in Numbers 25?
short_answer: It is highly unlikely because the geography and chronology do not fit Merneptah's campaign.
expanded_answer: The Numbers 25 plague is located east of the Jordan near the King's Road, beyond Moab, and Merneptah's campaign does not appear to have gone there. There is also a chronological problem: the plague would likely predate Merneptah's reign, while the Israel reference belongs to Merneptah's later campaign.

question: Which makes more sense, Merneptah going east of Moab or Ramesses II destroying Jericho?
short_answer: Neither option makes much sense.
expanded_answer: Both proposals were treated as bad explanations. In context, Merneptah going east of Moab fails geographically and chronologically, while the suggested Ramesses II explanation was not presented as a good alternative either.

question: How valuable would amber be in the time of Moses?
short_answer: The value is hard to know because amber was not meaningfully present or traded in Egypt at that time.
expanded_answer: Amber was primarily associated with northern Europe and was not meaningfully present in Egypt as a local material or import. Because no Egyptian amber jewelry or even clear evidence of an Egyptian term for it could be found, its value in Egypt is hard to estimate.

question: Were Egyptian trees capable of producing amber?
short_answer: No. Egypt lacked the coniferous forests associated with amber formation.
expanded_answer: Amber comes from particular coniferous tree resins that fossilized under past conditions, and Egyptian trees were not thought capable of producing it. Egypt did not have coniferous forests like the Baltic region, so there was no local natural source for amber.

question: Is belief in corruption of human nature necessary for Christians?
short_answer: Inherited corruption is not mandatory, but federative responsibility and inherent corruption are hard to avoid.
expanded_answer: Inherited corruption, federative responsibility, and inherent corruption were distinguished. Christians need not hold a specific inherited-corruption view of original sin, but the Old Testament bakes in corporate responsibility going back to Adam, and human beings plainly show an inherent propensity toward sin and rebellion.

question: Why did ancient Israelite military strategy favor slingers over archers?
short_answer: Stones and slings were cheap and easy to make, while bows and arrows required more specialized skill.
expanded_answer: Slings were accessible because stones were everywhere, leather slings were easy to make, and ordinary youths or shepherds could practice with them. Arrows, arrowheads, bows, and accurate archery required much more skill and training, so archers were not as universally available.

question: Did soldiers make leather slings themselves, or did other people make the leather for them?
short_answer: Soldiers generally could craft their own slings, and many people knew how to tan hides.
expanded_answer: A sling was a weapon ordinary people could make, and once made it did not wear out quickly. Because many people in that setting likely knew how to tan hides, slingers did not need a highly specialized production system comparable to archery equipment.

question: Did David ever try to contact Michael Heiser about the claim that a 13th-century Exodus makes nothing in the Bible line up?
short_answer: David and Heiser never actually met, though people tried to put them in the same room.
expanded_answer: They were described as passing ships in the night: they overlapped around lectures and podcasts but never had the conversation. In David's assessment, Heiser was wrong on the Exodus, partly because of strong influence from David Rohl's revised chronology, while still doing valuable work in other areas.

question: What sci-fi or fantasy settings, themes, or plots are underexplored, and which should be given a break?
short_answer: Underexplored areas include new worlds, older and married characters, and serious worldbuilding; gender exploration and wandering-space-hobo plots need a break.
expanded_answer: Science fiction and fantasy often neglect older characters, married couples, older single people, consistent economies, and interesting military or social systems. The desired direction was more exploration of new worlds and concepts and less repetitive treatment of gender themes or familiar roaming-space-adventurer patterns.

question: Do older authors also underrepresent old people in their writing?
short_answer: Yes. Many older writers still underrepresent older characters because youth feels more exciting to them.
expanded_answer: Some older writers relive their younger years in fiction, so they still center young characters. Writers who embrace older characters can give them clearer goals, stronger guardrails from life experience, and more gravitas when they grow.

question: Does Isaiah 13:17-19 contradict history about the Medes attacking Babylon?
short_answer: The text first speaks of Babylonians rather than only the city, so the supposed contradiction needs the passage read carefully.
expanded_answer: Verses 17-18 were read as about the Babylonians generally, not specifically the city of Babylon, so Opis can satisfy that attack language. Verse 19 compares Babylon's fall to Sodom and Gomorrah, which fits overthrow rather than a wall siege: a sudden takeover rather than a formal attack on the city.

question: Did the Medes and Persians attack Babylon eventually?
short_answer: Only in the broad sense of invading it; Babylon's fall was described more as a takeover than a siege or attack.
expanded_answer: The Medes and Persians got into the city and killed important soldiers, guards, and officials, but the city was not taken by a normal siege of the walls. For that reason, it was better described as a takeover than an attack in the sense assumed by the objection.

question: How does David stay focused on goals amid many battles and distractions for Christians?
short_answer: Refuse distraction, pick battles carefully, and focus on work that builds something useful.
expanded_answer: Many online disputes are driven by attention-seeking and do not resolve anything even if one wins them. The priority is writing, research, publishing, and work that builds up the kingdom, so petty fights that waste time are avoided.

question: What videos would David like to popcorn review but cannot because of copyright concerns?
short_answer: Examples include *The Ten Commandments*, A&E material such as ancient aliens content, and older films like *The Mummy*.
expanded_answer: The YouTube copyright detection system makes some material too difficult to review even after stripping it down. *The Ten Commandments* was named as a desired review because of its strengths, but that and similar studio-protected material trigger copyright enforcement too aggressively.

question: Are there literary techniques from the Bible that could be used more in fiction?
short_answer: Most biblical techniques are general literary techniques, though chiasm and structural reflection could be used more.
expanded_answer: The Bible uses many techniques also found in broader literature. Chiasm may be more characteristic of ancient literature and could be used structurally in modern fiction, but modern fiction is often more asymmetrical; mirrored movement around a climax was also offered as a useful possibility.

question: What are the seven seals, and why must someone worthy open them?
short_answer: Revelation is cyclical, the seals mark a sealed scroll, and only one with authority, holiness, and worthiness can open it.
expanded_answer: Revelation was explained as cycling through the same events from different angles. The seals are clay-seal style closures on a scroll, and opening them carries the responsibility of consummating the ordained course of history; only Christ, as the victorious lion and slain lamb with authority, holiness, power, and worthiness, can open it.

question: Does Genesis 1 teach creation ex nihilo or ex materia, and would an ex materia reading make the God-creation relationship like Egyptian or Babylonian god-human relationships?
short_answer: Genesis 1 does not clearly teach creation ex nihilo, and an ex materia reading would not necessarily make those relationships equivalent.
expanded_answer: Genesis 1 and most of the Old Testament do not clearly state creation from nothing. Hebrews 11:3 comes closest, though the answer connected it more with passages about God stretching out the heavens than with Genesis 1 directly. The proposed equivalence with Egyptian or Babylonian divine-human relationships was rejected as not necessarily following, but that point was not developed further.

question: How prominent were Semites in the Delta after Avaris, including Dynasty 19?
short_answer: There were Semites outside Avaris, especially Wadi Tumilat, but most left after Avaris; a smaller presence remained at Thebes.
expanded_answer: There were significant Semitic populations beyond Avaris, especially in Wadi Tumilat because its pools supported sheep grazing, with some also south of the Pelusiac estuary and in western Thebes. question: Is the 12th-century Exodus proposed by Rendsburg and Bietak persuasive?
