Moses is an example of a name with an Egyptian theophoric element removed, and other names could have been similarly adjusted. Because the biblical record may preserve later Yahwistic forms, those names alone do not prove pre-exodus Yahweh worship.

episode_title: Understanding Hell, There Will Be A Test.
question: Did Egypt or Israel have anything like chess?
short_answer: No exact equivalent existed; Egyptian senet is the closest comparison, but it was a different kind of game.
expanded_answer: There was no real equivalent to chess in Egypt or Israel. The closest Egyptian comparison is senet, a race-type board game with multiple pieces, but its rules are not fully known and it is not chess. Chess itself developed much later in the Islamic period and was then adapted in Europe.

episode_title: Understanding Hell, There Will Be A Test.
question: How did the Israelites move the parts of the tabernacle?
short_answer: The tabernacle was modular, built to be dismantled and carried in assigned sections by Levites.
expanded_answer: The tabernacle is described as a modular tent structure with beams, crossbeams, poles, and fabric that could be taken down, rolled up, carried, and reassembled. Different Levitical clans had different responsibilities: some set it up and took it down, others carried it, and Aaron's family handled priestly service. Its design was therefore meant for transport, not permanent construction.

episode_title: Understanding Hell, There Will Be A Test.
question: Have you seen Galil's Facebook post about his readings of the tablets?
short_answer: The readings look increasingly untenable to other scholars, and the episode is described as a growing embarrassment.
expanded_answer: The broader Galil situation is described as embarrassing because scholars are increasingly saying they cannot see how his photographs support his readings. Peter van der Veen no longer appears to agree with Galil on key details, undermining the claim of a unified epigraphic team. The assessment is that the claims are falling apart before peer-reviewed publication.

episode_title: Understanding Hell, There Will Be A Test.
question: What is your opinion of sand?
short_answer: He likes sand, especially for excavation, and much prefers working in Egyptian sand to Israeli mud.
expanded_answer: Sand is praised as clean, easy to sweep, shovel, sift, and even use to rub dirt from the hands. Egyptian sand is contrasted with Israeli caked mud, which is described as unpleasant to dig through, and tar is worse still because it requires solvents. For an Egyptologist, liking sand is treated as practically necessary.

episode_title: Understanding Hell, There Will Be A Test.
question: What is your opinion of near-death experiences?
short_answer: Near-death experiences are not actual death, often involve immediate terror before later reinterpretation, and remain medically and theologically unresolved.
expanded_answer: Near-death experiences are not full death because clinical death is not the same as neural death; the neural pathways have not degraded. Reports are noted in which patients initially describe terror, torment, or fire shortly after revival, then later reinterpret the experience as beautiful. The phenomenon is treated as real but unresolved, needing medical, psychological, and theological analysis rather than simple proof-texting.

episode_title: Understanding Hell, There Will Be A Test.
question: Is it a sin for Christians to get tattoos?
short_answer: Not necessarily; the ancient ban was tied to ceremonial law and pagan dedication, so wisdom now depends on cultural context and conscience.
expanded_answer: The ancient prohibition is explained in terms of tattoos as religious dedication marks to other gods, including examples from Egyptian priestesses. For Christians, the ceremonial law is covered by Christ, so tattoos are not inherently sinful. Whether getting one is wise depends on cultural meaning: a military tattoo may be harmless, a tattoo in a context where it signals organized crime may be unwise, and modern memorial tattoos raise questions of conscience and context.

question: Have you considered doing a tutorial series on archaeological methods or the historical method?
short_answer: A methods project has been considered, especially on archaeological fallacies, but other book projects come first.
expanded_answer: An archaeological-methods project is on the wishlist, and a publisher had asked about a possible book on archaeological fallacies analogous to historians' fallacies. The priority remains other planned books, especially chronology and the plagues of the Exodus, because limited writing time keeps pushing methods work back.

question: Does the problem of evil go beyond Christianity, and do atheists face their own version of it?
short_answer: Yes: atheists face a problem of defining evil without an all-good standard, though it is not identical to the theistic problem.
expanded_answer: The theistic problem sets an all-good God against evil's existence; the atheistic problem is definitional. Atheism can treat evil as a brute fact, but without an all-good reference point it struggles to define good and evil beyond subjective harm or a low comparative standard.

question: Is the Samaritan Pentateuch older and more accurate than the Masoretic Text?
short_answer: It is probably older, perhaps by a few centuries, but older does not automatically mean more accurate; he still finds it very useful for textual criticism.
expanded_answer: The Samaritan Pentateuch probably branched off earlier than the Masoretic tradition and may even be older than the Septuagint in some form, with Samaritan-type readings represented among the Dead Sea Scrolls. But age is not the same as accuracy, and scholars such as Emanuel Tov treat the Masoretic tradition as remarkably consistent over time, so the Samaritan Pentateuch is valuable alongside the Masoretic Text, Septuagint, and Dead Sea Scrolls rather than automatically superior.

question: What is Yahweh's essence, how can it be one if there are other gods, and what do "essence" and "person" mean for God?
short_answer: Only a brief answer is given: God's essence is his indivisible fullness or immensity, while the persons are distinct hypostases within that one divine essence.
expanded_answer: Patristic theological language describes a divine person as a hypostasis while warning against treating God as having separable parts. God's essence is the wholeness, oneness, or immensity of God, while other beings called gods are powerful but finite spirits or powers; the answer also distinguishes the common plural use of `elohim` from the magnificent plural applied to Yahweh as the greatest God.

question: Why do Genesis 10:19, Genesis 17:8, and Numbers 34 describe different borders for Canaan and the promised land?
short_answer: Later historical realities matter: Philistine control, the allotment to Abraham's wider descendants, and Israel's own disobedience all affect how the land is described and occupied.
expanded_answer: The passages overlap but describe different contexts. The Genesis promise to Abraham is broader than what Israel later occupies, since related peoples such as Edom, Moab, and Aram also receive portions as Abraham's descendants, while Philistine control of the coastal plain and Israel's own failure or disobedience also affect what Israel actually secures.

question: In Hebrew, does placing `he` after an `a` sound always produce an `o` sound, and why is `Elohim` pronounced that way rather than `Lahem`?
short_answer: No confident general rule is offered; tentatively, the `o` in `Elohim` functions as a helper vowel, but comparative Semitics is outside his strongest area.
expanded_answer: He does not give a confident general explanation for the proposed consonant-and-vowel pattern. The tentative answer is that the `o` in `Elohim` functions as a helper vowel that eases the transition between syllables, but comparative Semitics is not his strongest field and a Hebrew linguist might give a better technical account.

question: Could Cyaxares II be Darius the Mede in Daniel 5:31?
short_answer: He does not link them confidently; he prefers keeping the disputed identifications separate and leans instead toward Darius as a Median name for Cyrus.
expanded_answer: Both Cyaxares II and Darius the Mede are controversial, and linking two controversial identifications together does not make the case stronger. D. J. Wiseman's proposal that kings could have different names for different kingdoms or settings seems more plausible to him, possibly with Darius as a Median name for Cyrus, but he says there is not enough information to be confident.

question: How would you refute the full preterist claim that Isaiah 65:20 rules out a physical resurrection?
short_answer: Full preterism is rejected strongly, and Isaiah's prophetic language can be read as poetic or transitional rather than as a denial of bodily resurrection.
expanded_answer: The resurrection itself is the main refutation: if believers are not bodily raised like Christ, death has not really been conquered and Christ's completed work is undermined. Isaiah 65:20 is treated as prophetic and poetic language, with the hundred-year-old youth functioning as a contrast about life and immortality rather than a straightforward denial of bodily resurrection.

question: Could near-death experiences be supernatural, with consciousness partly entering the afterlife and then returning?
short_answer: It is impossible to say with confidence, but he does not want to rule out the possibility that consciousness can leave the body and return.
expanded_answer: Evaluating near-death experiences would require retroductive reasoning: asking what the world would have to be like for the experience to be true. Consciousness might leave the body and return, but evidence is hard to obtain, the person is not yet fully dead in a near-death experience, and the likelihood remains unclear.

question: Have you heard of yacon syrup?
short_answer: No; it was new to him, and the on-stream lookup made it unlikely to fit his diabetes diet.
expanded_answer: Yacon syrup is looked up during the livestream and identified as a sweetener made from a tuberous root, somewhat like syrup. Because the information found mentions substantial fructose and free glucose, it is probably not something he could use while managing diabetes by diet, though he appreciates learning about new sugar substitutes.

question: What are your thoughts on 1 Corinthians 11:3-6?
short_answer: The passage uses a culturally specific head-covering practice to discuss headship as responsibility, not tyrannical authority, while also noting women praying and prophesying in public.
expanded_answer: Paul uses a time-and-place-specific head-covering practice to communicate a broader point about authority and responsibility. The passage shows women praying and prophesying publicly, recognizes that customs changed across Jewish and Christian settings, and frames headship as a hierarchy of responsibility in which men are called to shepherd, teach, and care for their households.

question: Why did David pick up five stones when he went to fight Goliath?
short_answer: Goliath had brothers, David may have been prepared for more than one opponent, and the stones were large practical sling stones rather than tiny pebbles.
expanded_answer: David may have carried five stones because Goliath had brothers and because five was probably a practical number to carry. It also corrects the common picture of tiny pebbles, describing the sling stones as large, roughly baseball-sized rocks that would hit more like small cannonballs.

question: After finishing Joshua and moving into Judges, what should a reader keep in mind?
short_answer: Both books are arranged pedagogically from better to worse rather than simply chronologically, with tribal and judge sequences carrying theological meaning.
expanded_answer: Joshua and Judges are arranged to teach, not simply to provide strict chronology. Joshua moves through tribal material from better to worse, and Judges similarly moves from better judges to worse ones, with overlapping episodes rather than a single linear narrative; by the time the reader reaches Jephthah and Samson, the deterioration is part of the book's point.

question: Are there records of 185,000 Assyrians being killed or dying by disease while besieging Jerusalem in 2 Kings 19:35?
short_answer: The Bible uniquely records the deaths, while Sennacherib's own records sound evasive; he thinks a major loss, possibly by plague, fits the evidence but cannot be proved in detail.
expanded_answer: Several historical sources discuss Sennacherib's siege, but the Bible is the source that records the deaths. Sennacherib's prism instead presents Hezekiah as trapped while avoiding any clear account of taking Jerusalem, receiving tribute, or bringing the king back in chains, which he reads as evasive spin consistent with a major setback, perhaps from disease, though the exact mechanism cannot be established.

question: What are your thoughts on baptismal regeneration, and is baptism salvific directly or indirectly?
short_answer: In his view, baptism itself is not salvific directly or indirectly, but it is a necessary act of obedience and an important sign of Christian faith.
expanded_answer: Denominational answers differ, with Lutheran, Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant, and baptism-essentialist positions all mentioned. His own view is that the Holy Spirit regenerates at salvation rather than through the act of baptism itself; baptism is still very important as a first act of obedience, and refusing it raises spiritual concerns, but he does not treat it as saving.

question: Can Revelation 12 be used to determine the birth date of Jesus, as Bullinger and Heiser suggest?
short_answer: Revelation 12 and constellation alignments do not establish a precise birth date; that kind of archaeoastronomy is treated as highly unreliable.
expanded_answer: Revelation 12 does not seem to provide a direct birth-date indicator, and the argument is recognized as depending on constellation alignments. That method is treated as highly unreliable because archaeoastronomy often sounds scientific but depends on uncertain observation points, elevations, and reference assumptions, making exact dates from ancient alignments effectively pseudoscientific in his view.

question: If you were in ancient Egypt and commanded to share Yahweh with Egyptians, what would be an effective evangelistic strategy?
short_answer: Ancient Egypt would be difficult mission ground because the issue is an entire religious culture, not a simple individual appeal.
expanded_answer: A Yahweh worshiper would be confronting state cults, local gods, household shrines, and private piety. The suggested strategy is to remove idols from the household shrine, creating a visible but nonviolent cultural disruption that prompts questions and opens conversation, while recognizing that Egypt allowed more private religious variety than some other ancient settings.

question: Does burning in Daniel 3 have a more substantial Egyptian background than Babylonian, Persian, or Greek backgrounds?
short_answer: Egyptian religion does use fire imagery for punishment and purification, but the Daniel 3 furnace itself was likely a Babylonian furnace for destroying sacred furniture and recovering metal.
expanded_answer: Egyptian fire motifs include punishment imagery and purification through incense smoke, but Daniel 3 is read in a Babylonian setting. Such furnaces could have destroyed captured sacred furniture, burned away wood, and recovered bronze, silver, or gold to pay soldiers, which fits the large furnace imagery better than a specifically Egyptian background.

question: Was the Egyptian opening-of-the-mouth ritual used for idols as well as mummies, and does the creation of man allude to it?
short_answer: Yes: the rite could be used on mummies, idols, sacred furniture, and temples, and Genesis' creation imagery does allude to the idea of spirit entering a lifeless formed body.
expanded_answer: Opening-of-the-mouth rites allowed the spirit of the dead to reinhabit, leave, and receive sustenance through a mummy's body. The same logic could inaugurate idols, sacred furniture, thrones, shrines, and temples, and Genesis' formation of man from earth followed by divine breath evokes the idea of a lifeless formed body receiving spirit through mouth or nostrils.

question: Is there archaeological or historical confirmation of the war machines described in 2 Chronicles 26:15?

question: Were noses removed from Egyptian statues as a reversal of the opening-of-the-mouth ritual?

question: What is the difference between a book and a codex?

question: If parapsychology is often considered pseudoscience, why do you take any of it seriously?

question: Why is "Red Sea" considered an error in Exodus?

question: If the census number 603,550 in Numbers 1 only works by rethinking terms like clans and hundreds, how do you make the census work?

question: How did the Egyptians view numbers: literally or symbolically, and did that influence the ages of the patriarchs in Genesis 5 and 11?

expanded_answer: Genesis 5 and 11 are treated separately from Egyptian number symbolism because the patriarchal ages are read as the lifespans of clan lines rather than single individuals. Egyptian numbers could function as mathematical data, regnal-year counts, symbolic language such as "million years" for enduring mortuary temples, or patterned numerology such as the 400th year, fourth month, and fourth day. Like numbers in other languages, their meaning depended on context. The succession-list structure does not require each named son to be the individual immediately begotten in the preceding line; the final links in Genesis 5 and 11 give younger sons honorific positions, supporting a clan-line reading across generations.

question: How did Moses know the events of Genesis 1 through 11?
short_answer: Earlier generations handed the material down, and Moses recorded inherited material in the New Kingdom period, likely around the 13th century BC.

The core writing of Genesis is dated to the Egyptian New Kingdom, likely the 13th century BC, partly because Egyptian terms such as "Pharaoh" appear in Genesis even though the term belongs to a later Egyptian setting than the events described. Moses received inherited material and made it permanent in written form.

question: If the promised-land border is the Brook of Egypt, is its limit the main channel or the entire catchment, and could it include the Sinai mines at Serabit?

The wording "up to" the brook is treated as an exclusive limit rather than permission to push the border deeply into Sinai.

question: Did the writer of Hebrews know the judges' order, and if Judges presents a decline from better to worse judges, why are Samson and Jephthah still included in Hebrews 11?

It selects individual acts of faith that God used, such as Samson trusting God at the end and Jephthah ultimately trusting God for victory, even though both men were deeply flawed. question: What role do you think Solomon played in the writing of Ecclesiastes?

question: What did the career of an Old Testament prophet actually look like: was he a street preacher all day, or more like C. S. Lewis writing and speaking at conferences of tribal leaders?
short_answer: Many prophets mainly settled disputes and clarified present situations; some came through prophetic schools, while others kept ordinary day jobs.

The schools produced both prophets and support personnel, including scribes and other helpers, while called prophets often served part-time. Most prophetic work was not dramatic future prediction but ordinary mediation, arbitration, and "forth telling," meaning clarifying the present situation and God's perspective. Levites, not prophets, more closely filled the ordinary public teaching or street-preaching role.

question: In Numbers 31:3, 7-11, Moses fights Midian even though his wife and in-laws were Midianites. Does that mean he betrayed his own family?

question: How should someone respond to militant Messianic Jews who say Sabbath must be Saturday and that Sunday church is satanic?

question: Is a hot dog a sandwich?

question: How does the Old Testament inform church structure today, including priests, the pope, prophets, apostles, and related offices?

question: You mentioned Hebrew was lost and recovered twice. Can you explain the circumstances?
short_answer: Hebrew first ceased as a living language after the Roman dispersions and was revived in the Masoretic era, then later declined again before modern Zionism revived it as a spoken language.
expanded_answer: Hebrew was first lost as a living language after the Roman dispersions, especially after Bar Kokhba, as Jewish communities were scattered and Hebrew survived more as a scriptural language. That revival did not permanently hold as Jewish communities shifted into Arabic and European languages, and Hebrew was revived again in the 19th-century Zionist movement as a modern spoken language for a homeland.

question: In 2 Kings 2:23-24, is it possible that the 42 youths were threatening Elisha rather than merely taunting him?

question: Do you think Neferneferuaten was Nefertiti?

question: What punishments were there in Egypt for offending or insulting the king, and for other crimes? Are there any good resources on this?

question: What are your thoughts on the eruv wires around places like Manhattan?
short_answer: Eruv wires are a creative legal workaround that symbolically encloses an area where carrying is allowed on the sabbath.
expanded_answer: An eruv is explained as a later Jewish legal construction based on posts and a beam, with a wire serving as the beam. Since carrying within one's house is allowed under that interpretation, the eruv symbolically treats a larger district as an enclosed space. Telephone or utility wires can become part of the enclosure, allowing very large urban eruv areas.

question: Is dividing Old Testament laws into cultural, moral, and cultic categories a helpful method or just a trick to dismiss laws people dislike?
short_answer: The categories are imperfect but legitimate when handled with context, since not all laws function the same way.
expanded_answer: No categorization of Old Testament law is perfect, but distinctions can still be useful. Many laws functioned as case law or guidance for judges, and many commandments were tied specifically to temple, tabernacle, sacrifice, and ceremonial practice. The categories become irresponsible if used to discard disliked laws casually, but they are not inherently a cheap trick because laws have different contexts and functions.

question: In Judges 1:7, were Adoni-bezek's seventy kings really heads of families or more like village rulers?
short_answer: They were probably rulers of many small towns or villages, and the count could even include repeat conquests of the same places.
expanded_answer: The passage is read as referring to kings of small settlements rather than mere family heads. Ancient agrarian populations were spread through many small villages and towns, so seventy local rulers in a region is plausible. The tally could also include repeated conquest of the same town after rebellion, with a newly installed ruler later defeated and added to Adoni-bezek's count.

question: What were the grievous infirmities of Egypt in Deuteronomy 7:15?
short_answer: The phrase is treated as a broad reference to Egypt's severe disease environment rather than one precisely identifiable illness.
expanded_answer: The verse does not name a single disease, so the answer treats it as a broad bucket for Egypt's known health burdens. Examples include polluted Nile water, parasites, intestinal disease, lesions, sores, flies, mosquito-borne illnesses, sexually transmitted diseases, malnutrition, arthritis, tooth decay, abscesses, and periodic plagues. The point is the wider Egyptian disease environment Israel knew from experience.

question: What is going on with Gideon's ephod in Judges 8:27?
short_answer: Gideon makes a cultic ritual garment he should not be making, and its display becomes idolatrous apparatus and a snare.
expanded_answer: An ephod is described as a ritual garment, a vest or vest-kilt form associated with priestly and divine imagery. Gideon's problem is that he makes such an object from the gold and displays it in Ophrah, where it becomes associated with idolatrous cult apparatus. Although the high priest had an ephod, Gideon had no business making this kind of object for himself, and the cultural context made it easy to treat as a new idol or cultic focus.

question: Are fortune cookies a form of divination, and should Christians avoid them?
short_answer: No, unless someone is treating them seriously as divination; ordinarily they are just playful sayings in cookies.
expanded_answer: Fortune cookies are not divination in ordinary use because no one is appealing to a deity or serious spiritual power to reveal the future. Most fortunes are generic sayings or playful aphorisms that can be interpreted many ways. Christians should avoid using them as divination if they are actually treating them as guidance for the future, but otherwise they are harmless and unserious.

question: In Exodus 25:9, is the tabernacle or its furniture just a scale model of a larger heavenly structure?
short_answer: The simple scale-model reading is not convincing; the sacred furniture also functions as a real divine-human interface.
expanded_answer: Exodus 25:9 is read in the context of the tabernacle and ark instructions, where the ark's dimensions are reasonable for an actual ritual object rather than merely a reduced model. The mercy seat or sacred furniture may in some sense represent a larger divine throne room, as ancient sacred objects could be models. Yet the Shekinah glory was understood to be present between the cherubim, so the ark functioned as a real point of interface between God and Israel, not only as a miniature.

question: Does Job 33:22-24 have christological overtones, and what should we make of Elihu's role there?
short_answer: The christological reading is possible, but interpretation of Elihu is highly contested and the answer remains deliberately cautious.
expanded_answer: Some exegetes see christological overtones in the mediator and ransom language, while others view Elihu as an overconfident younger speaker whose role is ambiguous. Elihu is not condemned the way the other comforters are, but the passage remains difficult. A firm conclusion is declined, leaving the christological reading possible rather than settled.

question: Is the story that someone found a golden ass image in the Jerusalem temple a fabrication, or does it connect to Seth or Hyksos traditions?
short_answer: It is probably ideological fabrication, and the Jerusalem temple would not normally have housed that kind of animal image.
expanded_answer: Hyksos worship is associated with Baal in the cited evidence, while the golden donkey story is treated as polemic. Seleucid-era writers had ideological reasons to portray Judeans as corrupt or ridiculous, especially during struggles over control of the high priesthood. Jerusalem's temple culture was acutely sensitive to animal imagery, as shown by reactions to Herod's Roman eagle, so a normal golden animal image inside the temple is unlikely, though unrelated looted treasure near the precinct remains a remote possibility.

question: What is the best explanation for the discrepancy between Jesus' genealogies in Matthew and Luke?
short_answer: No firm answer is given because genealogies often serve non-obvious literary and theological purposes, and these two require closer study.
expanded_answer: Matthew's and Luke's genealogies are not adjudicated in detail. Genealogies are not always simple pedigree lists; they can communicate posterity, theological meaning, and literary purposes that are not immediately intuitive. Because genealogies contain interpretive traps, a confident explanation is deferred until closer study.

question: Did Pharisees in the New Testament period believe their traditions came directly from Moses, and when did the traditions of the elders become the oral law?
short_answer: The written oral law emerges in the post-70 AD rabbinic period, and Pharisees likely distinguished elder traditions from the Torah itself.
expanded_answer: The second part is answered first: after the temple's destruction in AD 70 and later upheavals, rabbis began preserving traditions in writing because the temple system and Sadducean role had collapsed. Mishnah, Talmud, and related rabbinic material are placed roughly from the second century onward. For New Testament Pharisees, the traditions of the elders were important, but the answer does not present them as already identical to the later written oral law or as direct Mosaic dictation.

question: What relationship would Moshe have had to Ramesses? Was it really brotherly?
short_answer: Probably not brotherly; Moses was likely older and shared parts of the same household world without being a close same-age sibling figure.
expanded_answer: The reconstruction places Ramesses II in the Ramesside household around Avaris before the family gained royal status. Moses may have been adopted into that wider household world, but he would likely have been at least a decade older and trained differently. The relationship may have involved overlapping court, scribal, and household circles, not the intimate brotherly relationship common in popular retellings.

question: In Judges 8, why does Gideon kill the men of Penuel but not the men of Succoth when the offense seems similar?
short_answer: The likely difference is the aftermath: Succoth seems to give up its leaders, while Penuel stands behind its resistance and tower; some speculation remains.
expanded_answer: Judges 8 shows both Succoth and Penuel refusing support to Gideon's exhausted men. The later difference may be that Succoth's leaders are identified and handed over for punishment, while Penuel's tower and community resistance indicate a broader corporate stand against Gideon. The explanation is presented as plausible rather than certain because the text does not spell out every detail.

question: If I attend a local Messianic Jewish congregation, how do I avoid being "that Gentile"?
short_answer: Behave normally and respectfully, avoid cosplay and overperforming Jewish identity, and be sensitive to congregational customs, especially around food.
expanded_answer: Drawing on experience in a Messianic Jewish congregation, the answer warns against conspicuous overperformance: dressing up, adopting exaggerated markers of Jewish identity, or trying to out-Jewish the congregation. Practical advice includes acting normally, respecting the community's customs, and being considerate with food and kosher sensitivities at potlucks. The core point is humility and sensitivity rather than performative identity.

question: Why is Pascha or Easter celebrated on Sunday rather than on a fixed calendar date?
short_answer: Easter is tied to Sunday because of the resurrection, while different Christian traditions calculate the date differently in relation to the lunar calendar and Passover.
expanded_answer: Easter is always on Sunday because Christians are celebrating the day Jesus rose from the dead. Passover follows the Jewish calendar and does not always fall on Sunday, while Christian liturgical calendars calculate Easter by lunar rules that are not recited from memory here. Eastern and Western traditions can calculate the date differently, and Easter can sometimes coincide with Passover but does not have to.

question: Are mayonnaise, kosher salt, and pickles actually kosher?
short_answer: Mayonnaise and pickles are generally kosher, while "kosher salt" is named for its use in koshering rather than special status as salt.
expanded_answer: Mayonnaise is treated as kosher because its basic ingredients are egg, oil, spices, vinegar, or lemon juice. "Kosher salt" is explained as shorthand for koshering salt: a flaky, non-iodized salt used to draw liquid from meat during the koshering process. The salt itself is not uniquely kosher, and the same kind of salt can also be used for pickles, which are generally kosher.

question: If Moshe had not parted the Reed Sea, why could the Israelites not just go around the Yam Suph?
short_answer: They were boxed in and could not outrun Pharaoh's chariots; the route itself functions as a divine trap for the Egyptian army.
expanded_answer: The Yam Suph is described as part of a massive estuary at the Pelusiac branch of the Nile, thousands of square miles in extent though not very deep. The Israelites were between the sea, wilderness, and named locations, with Pharaoh's army effectively on top of them. They could not detour around such a large water system while being pursued by chariots; in this reading, the geography sets up the divine trap that destroys the Egyptian force.

question: Why do we not find chariots or evidence of them there after the crossing?
short_answer: Egyptian chariots were built largely from wood and leather, so wet estuary conditions would quickly destroy most evidence.
expanded_answer: Chariots would not preserve well because their main materials were wood and stretched leather. Once submerged and smashed around in flowing estuary water, the leather and wood would rot, bodies would be consumed or scattered, and material would wash downstream. Only sparse bronze fittings might remain, so recoverable chariot evidence is not expected.

question: How deep and wide was the Sea of Reeds?
short_answer: The Sea of Reeds is estimated as hundreds of miles wide and about 20 to 40 feet deep.
expanded_answer: The estimate gives a vast lateral extent but relatively shallow depth. The depth estimate is tied to sediment deposits and geological surveys in the region, including work connected to the Suez Canal area. The point is that the body of water could be enormous across while still being only about 20 to 40 feet deep.

question: If the wind blew from the east, how would the sea have split, and would the people have had to fight hurricane-force winds?
short_answer: The setdown effect would part the water roughly east to west and would require a strong wind, about 50 mph, not hurricane force.
expanded_answer: The east wind is connected to wind setdown studies in the eastern Nile region, where strong focused winds can move water and locally lower water levels. In this explanation, the water is pushed roughly east to west, creating a crossing from the southeastern side toward the southwestern side before the people turn toward the wilderness. For a 20- to 40-foot-deep body of water, the necessary wind is estimated around 50 mph: strong, but not hurricane force.

question: Why do Saul and David's world contain so many El and Baal names and fewer Yahwistic ones?
short_answer: The naming pattern fits a period of widespread idolatry and cultural fashion when Israel was not consistently faithful.
expanded_answer: The names are linked to the religious condition of the period coming out of Judges and into Samuel, when Israel is often described as disobedient and idolatrous. In that context, Baal and El names would be common, with El retaining some ambiguity because it could be associated with Yahweh. Naming is also treated partly as cultural fashion, not a clean measure of formal theology.

question: What resources are there for learning about continental young earth creationism?
short_answer: There are no clear resources to recommend because the movement tends to be niche, local, and not strongly organized around publishing.
expanded_answer: Continental young earth creationism is contrasted with American young earth creationism. The American movement is evangelistic, conference-driven, and supported by publishing houses, literature, theme parks, and media, while the continental version tends to be local, church- or society-based, and less interested in public outreach. Much of it circulates through tracts, photocopies, or borrowed American material, so no clear resource list is offered.

question: Cheddar or mozzarella?
short_answer: It depends entirely on the application, and neither is his overall favorite cheese.
expanded_answer: Cheddar is preferred for macaroni and cheese or cheese on toast, while mozzarella fits pizza, chicken Parmesan, and tomato-cucumber Italian salad. Fresh mozzarella is praised, but neither cheddar nor mozzarella is named as the favorite. Cambazola is identified as the favorite, with Stilton and Manchego also mentioned approvingly.

question: When new dynasties took the throne, how did they establish religious legitimacy after starting as ordinary people?
short_answer: New dynasties often linked themselves to royal ancestry, cults, king lists, or revered royal figures, though the projects were not always fully successful.
expanded_answer: Several legitimacy mechanisms are named: claiming descent from royal ancestors, inserting oneself into king lists, or venerating revered royal figures and their cults. Seti I's Abydos king list is used as an example of presenting continuity with earlier kings while excluding illegitimate ones, and Ramesses II's veneration of Ahmose-Nefertari attaches him to an older royal line. Such efforts did not always resolve political and priestly tensions, especially with Theban interests.

question: Did biblical authors have room in their thinking for corporate or group persons?
short_answer: Yes; clan and corporate responsibility are central to biblical thought, often more than modern Western individualism expects.
expanded_answer: Biblical authors often think in terms of clans, family groups, tribes, and nations rather than only isolated individuals. The law about an unsolved murder outside a city, where city elders ritually deny responsibility and make a sacrifice, illustrates corporate responsibility. Revelation's seven churches are also addressed as corporate bodies, and clan societies can bear consequences for the actions of members.

question: How do I become a New Testament scholar coming out of high school?
short_answer: Start with a credible bachelor's program, get Greek early, and expect a long path through graduate study and specialization.
expanded_answer: The recommended path begins with college, preferably a credible accredited bachelor's program in a humanities field such as philosophy or religious studies, while getting Greek as early as possible and also learning Hebrew. The usual route is described as a bachelor's degree, then one or two master's degrees such as an MDiv, ThM, or MA sequence, followed by PhD specialization in New Testament studies. The goal is training to handle the New Testament competently and accurately, and that takes time.

question: If the Bible says little about the physical origin of the universe, what does it say about the physical end of the universe?
short_answer: Scripture gives even less concrete physical detail about the end than about the beginning: the present creation passes away, believers remain with God, and the renewed creation is left vague.
expanded_answer: The Bible gives broad eschatological language rather than a physical model of the final universe. Believers will be with God, the old heavens and earth are rolled up and replaced by new heavens and a new earth, and 2 Peter speaks of fire, but the text does not spell out what the final physical state will be like.

question: What advice would he give amateur archaeologists who want to engage the material seriously without becoming professionals?
short_answer: Read constantly. Wide, disciplined reading of reports, articles, and books matters more than the formal credential by itself.
expanded_answer: Serious engagement requires time spent reading archaeological reports, peer-reviewed articles, books, and collected essays. A well-read amateur can engage the material better than a credentialed archaeologist who stops reading, because effectiveness comes from sustained familiarity with the scholarly literature.

question: Are readings like `Heights of David` and `Enclosure of Abraham` on Shoshenq I's Bubastite Portal real?
short_answer: The `Heights of David` reading is fairly strong, while the `Enclosure of Abraham` reading is possible but less certain because the sign group may also refer to `stallions`.

The `Enclosure of Abraham` reading near Hebron is not wild, but it is less secure because the same signs could be read as an enclosure of stallions; the claim was checked against the hieroglyphic text and found mostly true, with the Abraham reading hedged.

question: Are there ancient Egyptian or Near Eastern parallels to Joseph's silver divination cup in Genesis 44:5?
short_answer: Yes. Tutankhamun's alabaster divination cup is a real Egyptian example, though silver vessels were rarer and more likely to be recycled.
expanded_answer: Tutankhamun's alabaster cup is an extant Egyptian divination cup, with lotus handles and Thoth imagery fitting divinatory use. The surviving example is alabaster rather than silver, but silver was very rare and valuable in Egypt, so silver vessels were likely to be melted down and reused instead of surviving archaeologically.

question: Is the idea that the tabernacle was a huge circular yurt or dome plausible?
short_answer: No. The proposal is an engineer's fantasy that does not fit the biblical description or the need for portability.
expanded_answer: The theory imagined an enormous dome, roughly a hundred feet across and high, and came from an idealized structural-engineering model. Such a structure would not be portable and did not fit the text, so it was treated as bizarre rather than a plausible tabernacle reconstruction.

question: Are the genealogies in Matthew 1 and Luke 3 partly clan lists rather than only individual pedigrees?
short_answer: Partly. The early portions that draw on Genesis should still be read largely in clan terms, while later portions move more toward individuals.

Because Matthew 1 and Luke 3 draw on Genesis for their earlier names, those early entries are mostly read as clans, while the later portions are more individual.

question: How should the Jericho dating debate between about 1550 BC and about 1400 BC be reconciled, especially with the scarab of Amenhotep III?
short_answer: There is no real contradiction: a Middle Bronze destruction fits around 1550, later Late Bronze occupation existed, and newer work at Jericho undercuts the idea that the site was simply destroyed by Joshua around 1400.
expanded_answer: Kathleen Kenyon's 1550 date refers to the Middle Bronze destruction of City IV, while Bryant Wood's 1400 argument depends on reading later finds as proof that same destruction was Joshua's. Lorenzo Nigro's work points to Late Bronze fortifications and occupation, so the Amenhotep III scarab and Mycenaean pottery make sense in a later city that survived into the thirteenth century before later leveling.

question: Could mainstream scholarship eventually accept a historical Exodus and conquest without accepting the supernatural claims?
short_answer: In his view, the field is already moving that way, with more scholars willing to treat the events historically while bracketing miraculous interpretation.
expanded_answer: Biblical minimalism was much stronger when he first studied archaeology, but the field now has less consensus and more room for historical readings. Exodus language can be handled like Egyptian royal inscriptions filled with divine claims: a secular historian can accept that a migration and settlement happened without accepting the miracle claims, just as historians can accept historical elements in Ramesses II's Kadesh account without believing in Amun or Montu.

question: Is there any new archaeological evidence for Solomon?

question: What was happening when Rehoboam encountered Pharaoh Shishak, and did Shishak invade Jerusalem?
short_answer: Shishak approached Jerusalem, but Rehoboam paid him off, so the city was not invaded.

question: If Adam's 930 years are really a clan lifespan, how should Genesis 5:5 be understood?
short_answer: The text reflects clan continuity rather than one individual's literal age, tying this to broader ancient Near Eastern ideas about lineage, memory, and the survival of a named house.
expanded_answer: Hebrew grammar alone does not settle the issue because the missing piece is cultural context. Ancient ideas of bodily death, death of memory, and death of the name help explain how a clan named for Adam could be said to live as long as its direct family line and identity continued, with Genesis and Exodus genealogies giving hints that long spans can refer to clan continuity.

question: Should we expect to find Moses' name in hieroglyphs, and what might that name have looked like in Egyptian?

question: What should be made of the so-called Samson seal from Tel Beth-Shemesh?

question: Could someone say `I am` in ancient Hebrew without making a divine claim?
short_answer: Yes. Ordinary forms for `I am` existed, and the force of passages like John 8:58 depends on the specific divine verbal form being invoked.

question: What does he think of David Rohl's claim that Joseph's tomb has been identified?
short_answer: The claim is unconvincing because the tomb count is overstated, the context is wrong, and the dating is about a century too early for Joseph.

question: How does Israel's status as the chosen people relate to Messiah's coming and to Messianic believers?

question: Did the Egyptians adopt foreign gods or identify them with their own deities?
short_answer: Yes. Egypt regularly adopted foreign gods when they fit the wider polytheistic system, and later often merged foreign and Egyptian deities rather than claiming the foreign god had always been Egyptian.
expanded_answer: Egyptians readily adopted foreign gods when those gods did not disrupt the polytheistic system, with Bes, Reshef, Baal, and Astarte given as examples. In the Ptolemaic period, they might merge Greek and Egyptian gods as versions of the same deity, but usually not by claiming the foreign god had originally been Egyptian.

question: Is Leviticus 15:19 about menstrual blood polluting the land?
short_answer: No. Leviticus 15 is read as ritual language about normal and abnormal bodily states, not as a statement that menstrual blood pollutes the land.
expanded_answer: Leviticus 15 was read in context with male emissions and intercourse, with clean and unclean language describing normal and abnormal bodily states rather than land pollution. The menstrual period was framed as a ritually unclean state for a limited time, and the rule may also have functioned as a rest period in a hard ancient labor environment.

question: Was the star of Bethlehem present at Jesus' birth, and can it be used to date the birth?
short_answer: The star belongs to the Magi episode after the birth, not the stable scene, so it does not directly give a birth date.
expanded_answer: The Magi arrived well after the birth, when the family was already in a house, so the star belongs to that later visit rather than to the nativity scene. question: What might life have been like for Moses growing up among Egyptians but not as one of them?
short_answer: Moses likely grew up in the Ramesside household at Avaris, exposed both to elite Egyptian administration and to the surrounding Semitic-speaking local population.
expanded_answer: In this reconstruction, Moses likely grew up in the Ramesside household at the palace of Avaris, an administrative residence for Lower Egypt rather than the king's main palace. question: How do Exodus 25:9 and Hebrews 8:5 fit with the idea that the tabernacle design drew on Egyptian models?
short_answer: The tabernacle was a copy and shadow adapted to what the Israelites already knew, so God gave a pattern in culturally intelligible terms rather than a de novo heavenly replica.

question: Is Genesis 15:4-5 a theophany, and could this be the angel of the Lord?
short_answer: Genesis 15:4-5 is very likely a theophany; whether it is the angel of the Lord depends on how broadly that phrase is being used.
expanded_answer: The passage is read as the Lord directly manifesting and speaking to Abraham, so it is very likely a theophany. It could also be described as the angel or messenger of the Lord if that term is being used broadly for a divine manifestation, but that identification is less definite because the wording itself is broader.

question: How could Egypt have hyperinflation in a barter or precious-metal economy?
short_answer: Inflation can happen when goods become scarce relative to other goods, and Egypt's loss of tribute and food supply pressures made prices rise across the economy.
expanded_answer: Prices can rise either because currency increases or because the supply of goods falls. question: As a manual laborer, does he recommend manual labor for Christians today, and are coworkers more resistant to the world than white-collar workers?

question: Roughly when in Horemheb's reign would Moses have fled Egypt?
short_answer: Moses likely fled around the twelfth to fourteenth regnal year of Horemheb, still comparatively young rather than already forty in a literal sense.

question: Who wrote Genesis 1-11, when and where was it written, and why?
short_answer: Genesis 1-11 may draw on source documents from Moses or his scribes around the Exodus, later compiled and perhaps supplemented as a nation-building anti-myth.

The response did not treat Genesis as one linear composition: it pictured Joshua receiving collections of origin, Exodus, and law documents that later scribes might have supplemented. Genesis 1-11 was described as an anti-myth for a mixed multitude leaving Egypt, giving many peoples a shared origin story and theological framework that prepared them for tabernacle worship.

question: If later pharaohs could not build pyramids because of labor costs, why not use slaves or honor-based unpaid labor?
short_answer: Slaves and volunteers still had to be fed and supplied, so the real expense remained provisioning labor; later pyramids became cheaper, smaller, or were replaced by rock-cut tombs.
expanded_answer: Slave or volunteer labor was not free in practice because workers still needed food, clothing, and basic support, and in Egypt payment was often food. Cost-cutting changes included Middle Kingdom mudbrick pyramids, smaller pyramids, and eventually rock-cut tombs, while labor stoppages like Deir el-Medina were tied to disrupted food shipments.

question: What are the biggest misconceptions about ancient Egypt, and which one annoys him the most?
short_answer: The most annoying misconception was that Egypt had an ironclad empire; Egyptian power in Canaan was more like tribute hegemony than annexation or tight political control.
expanded_answer: Egypt's control of Canaan was framed not as an annexed, tightly governed empire but as a hegemony designed to extract tribute. The Amarna letters and small garrison towns show Egypt mainly wanted tribute collected and reported, with limited troops and bureaucrats enforcing a system more like pressure and extraction than full administrative rule.
